title: Most Distant Quasar Found by Euclid Telescope: Slow-Feeding Black Hole Needed Rapid Early Growth
excerpt: Most distant quasar found: ESA’s Euclid space telescope spotted J1504+6252, nicknamed Dun Aonghasa, at redshift 8.13, about 630 million years after the Big Bang. Its supermassive black hole weighs roughly 360 million Suns yet feeds at 12% to 44% of its Eddington limit, so it grew faster earlier,
content:
ESA's Euclid space telescope has found the most distant quasar known, J1504+6252, nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, at a redshift of 8.13, which means astronomers see it as it was about 630 million years after the Big Bang. The study in Astronomy & Astrophysics (volume 715, article A356) was announced Nov. 24 with releases from MPIA and the University of Hamburg, and it reports a black hole of roughly 360 million Suns that feeds well below its maximum rate. According to MPIA's Julien Wolf, that means it must have grown faster earlier in cosmic history, started out heavier, or both.

The result gives astronomers a concrete test of one of their open problems: how black holes reached hundreds of millions of Suns within the universe's first 630 million years. The paper says a star-sized seed would need extremely rapid and nearly uninterrupted growth to get this big in time, and that the discovery does not allow a robust distinction between the competing formation pathways.

It is the first quasar confirmed beyond redshift 8, and Euclid already held the earlier distance records at redshifts 7.77 and 7.69, set only months ago. The paper says the new object shifts the quasar frontier back by about 39 million years. Before Euclid's July results, only three quasars were known beyond redshift 7.5, and those results raised the count to seven quasars beyond redshift 7.5, with Dún Aonghasa now the first past redshift 8.

A quasar is the bright core of a galaxy where a supermassive black hole heats infalling gas until it outshines the host's stars. Lead author Julien Wolf is a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg and is now at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) in Garching.

Optical Dropout Search Flags One Candidate in 3,644 Square Degrees of Euclid Data

Euclid is a wide-field survey telescope, and its Wide Survey will cover about 14,000 square degrees of sky over its six-year mission, so finding a rare object means filtering an enormous number of sources. The team searched the sky available in August 2025: 3,644 square degrees.

The quasar stood out as an optical dropout. The expansion of the universe stretches its light so far that it is undetected in Euclid's visible-light I_E band, down to about magnitude 26.2, yet it appears in the infrared Y_E, J_E and H_E bands at magnitudes of 24.10, 22.96 and 22.67. The team applied three selection methods: an extreme-deconvolution algorithm, an XGBoost machine-learning classifier and a template-fitting code called LePhare.

Their three redshift estimates (8.20, 8.21 and 7.98) averaged to a photometric redshift of 8.13 with an uncertainty of 0.10. Photometric redshifts can be off by a wide margin, and spectroscopic measurements are the more reliable standard, which is why follow-up telescopes were needed.

Four Telescopes Confirm Redshift 8.13 as Webb Weighs Black Hole

The paper lists observations with the Keck Observatory on Jan. 18, the Hubble Space Telescope on May 12, the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) on May 15 and 16, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) on June 26. MPIA says the LBT confirmed the high redshift and Webb supplied the final redshift measurement; the release adds that Silvia Belladitta led the LBT follow-up.

The systemic redshift of 8.129 ± 0.005 comes from a narrow hydrogen-beta emission line in Webb's spectrum, because narrow lines trace gas that moves more gently than the fast-moving gas near the black hole. A systematic uncertainty of 150 km/s (about 336,000 mph) dominates the error.

The mass comes from the width of the broad hydrogen-beta line. A standard calibration gives about 360 million Suns, with other calibrations spanning 210 million to 780 million Suns, and estimates from a magnesium II line are consistent within their uncertainties. Webb's synthetic photometry matches Euclid's brightness measurements to within 0.1 magnitude in all three infrared bands.

Why Must Slow-Feeding Black Holes Have Grown Faster Earlier?

The Eddington limit marks the luminosity at which outward radiation pressure balances gravity pulling gas inward. Dún Aonghasa is feeding at 12% to 44% of that limit, depending on the mass calibration, and the paper describes it as powered by a mature accreting black hole that is not currently accreting close to the limit.

That is the tension. The paper's growth tracks start near redshift 20, roughly 450 million years before the quasar is seen, and it says mergers are unlikely by themselves to assemble a black hole this heavy. A seed of about 100 Suns left by a first-generation star would need extremely rapid and nearly uninterrupted growth, while continuous Eddington-limited growth from redshift 20 would require a seed near 100,000 Suns. Wolf says that the closer to the Big Bang such quasars appear, the faster their black holes must have grown, the heavier they began, or both.

Paper Says Seed Pathways Cannot Yet Be Told Apart

MPIA says the authors' latest results seem consistent with direct collapse, in which a massive gas cloud collapses straight into a heavy black hole that then keeps growing. Direct-collapse seeds are typically about 100,000 Suns, form from metal-free gas, and some simulations suggest they are very rare.

The paper itself is more cautious. It says the discovery does not enable robust distinction between formation pathways, and it weighs runaway collisions in dense nuclear star clusters and an illustrative history built on a 5,000-Sun primordial black hole. It also tests super-Eddington growth, in which a black hole temporarily feeds faster than its limit, but the authors caution that feedback can suppress growth and that spin-up would raise radiative efficiency. MPIA adds that primordial black holes, hypothetical objects formed just after the Big Bang, could matter if even more distant quasars are found.

Slow Feeder May Be Typical, Not Outlier, Widening Seed Problem

The authors suggest that the luminous quasars known from the reionization era may be the rapidly accreting end of a broader population of already massive black holes. They also say substantially brighter members may remain undiscovered.

If that holds, any seed theory would have to explain many massive early black holes rather than a handful of outliers. That reading is an inference from the paper's suggestion, not a statement by its authors.

Does Webb Hold Higher Redshift Record for Black Holes?

Webb has found accreting black holes at higher redshift, but the records are defined differently. The paper defines quasars as the most luminous persistent sources of radiation, hosting black holes of 100 million to 10 billion Suns, and calls J1504+6252 the most distant quasar currently known.

The X-ray-luminous black hole in galaxy UHZ1 sits at redshift 10.073 ± 0.002. Chandra and Webb data place it 470 million years after the Big Bang, and its mass is far lower, an estimated 40 million Suns if it feeds at the Eddington rate. The Euclid paper notes that UHZ1 has been interpreted as heavily obscured and says the active-nucleus interpretation remains debated. Whether it counts as a quasar depends on the definition used.

Mass Error, Lyman-Alpha Damping and Possible Lensing Limit Findings

The mass uncertainty is ±0.43 dex, a factor of nearly three either way, and the paper flags the uncertain applicability of low-redshift calibrations to a luminous quasar at redshift above 8. The hydrogen Lyman-alpha line shows a strongly damped Lyman-alpha profile that the paper connects to a proximate damped Lyman-alpha system.

The carbon IV line is shifted by about 3,500 km/s (roughly 7.8 million mph), which the authors attribute to possible nuclear outflows. Strong gravitational lensing is considered unlikely, although modest, unresolved magnification cannot be excluded.

Name Comes From Cliff-Top Fort on Inis Mór

The nickname honors a prehistoric cliff-top fort on Inis Mór, one of Ireland's Aran Islands. The Euclid announcement ties the name to the quasar's position at the current observational frontier of quasars, and the fort itself stands at the edge of a cliff 100 m (328 ft) high.

Forecast Expects Two to Six Quasars Beyond Redshift 8 in Searched Area

The paper scales a forecast of 8 to 23 quasars beyond redshift 8 across about 14,000 square degrees down to the 3,644 square degrees it searched, giving an expectation of two to six quasars. A University of Hamburg release says at most a few tens are expected in Euclid's entire survey. That leaves a limited number of such objects to find, though Euclid has announced 31 ancient quasars in about 1.5 years, and 12 at redshift 7 or higher were new.

Eduardo Bañados says it is unclear how far back such black holes exist and that Euclid has a good chance of finding the limit, and Silvia Belladitta suggests more distant discoveries could come sooner than expected. The comparison point is recent: on Nov. 10, NSF NOIRLab announced the oldest known compact quasar pair at a redshift of 6.08, about 900 million years after the Big Bang, roughly 270 million years later than Dún Aonghasa.

For now, one confirmed quasar beyond redshift 8 shows that very large black holes already existed when the universe was about 630 million years old. MPIA says the record tightens constraints on black hole formation scenarios, yet the paper says it cannot yet pick among them, and a black hole feeding at a modest rate today still has to be explained by faster growth before it.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do astronomers turn redshift 8.13 into 630 million years after the Big Bang?

Light from a source at redshift 8.13 arrives with wavelengths 9.13 times longer than emitted, because the wavelength ratio equals 1 + z. Converting that stretch to cosmic age requires a cosmological model, and the paper's 630 million years reflects such a calculation.

Why is Euclid good at finding the most distant quasars?

Quasars this distant are dim and shifted deep into the infrared, which suits Euclid's near-infrared instrument. Its Wide Survey also will cover about 14,000 square degrees, a large area in which to look for rare objects.

Does the Eddington limit cap how fast any black hole can grow?

Not strictly. Models of accretion disks allow luminosities 10 to 100 times the limit without instabilities. The paper tests such super-Eddington growth but warns that feedback can suppress growth and that spin-up may also limit it.

Does Dún Aonghasa prove heavy seeds formed by direct collapse?

No. MPIA says the findings seem consistent with direct collapse, but the paper says the discovery does not enable robust distinction among formation pathways.
